text: In one command: SET q <token> NX EX 300 sets the key only if it is absent and attaches the expiry atomically. Use this rather than SETNX followed by EXPIRE: if the client dies between those two calls, the lock never expires.
why: The board pseudo-code writes setnx(..., ex=300), which is not a real command signature; readers need the correct atomic form.

text: Redis docs say the lock value 'must be unique across all clients and all lock requests', for example 20 random bytes or a timestamp concatenated with a client ID. A bare host name is not enough when several processes or retries on one host can contend.
why: The owner check on release is only as good as the uniqueness of the stored ID.

text: Since Redis 8.4 the safe release needs no Lua: DELEX key IFEQ my_random_value deletes the key only if its value matches. On older versions use the get-compare-del Lua script with EVAL.
why: Current Redis (checked October 2026) has a built-in command for exactly this pattern.

text: The owner check prevents deleting someone else's lock, but it does not stop consumer 1 from continuing its work after its lock expired, while consumer 2 also works. The standard fix is a fencing token: a number that increases with each lock grant and is sent with every write, so the storage service rejects writes from an older holder.
why: Without this, learners think the safe release makes the timeout edge case fully safe.

text: Redlock's acquire rule has two conditions: the client locked a majority (at least 3 of 5) AND the total time spent acquiring is less than the lock validity time. The usable validity is then the TTL minus the time spent acquiring.
why: The elapsed-time check is the half of the algorithm the lecture skipped.

text: A client that fails to get the majority should try to unlock all instances, 'even the instances it believed it was not able to lock'. A SET may have succeeded even though its reply was lost. It should then retry after a random delay so that competing clients do not keep colliding.
why: Completes the failure path and explains the random backoff.

text: Redis's documented fix for this edge case is 'delayed restarts': keep a crashed instance unavailable for a bit longer than the max lock TTL, so every lock it held has expired before it rejoins. The alternative is AOF persistence with fsync=always, at a performance cost.
why: Gives the actual mitigation for the student's scenario instead of relying on low probability.

text: Redis's own Redlock page adds two consistency caveats. First, implement fencing tokens; don't assume a lock is retained as long as the process that acquired it is alive. Second, Redis does not use a monotonic clock for TTL expiry, so a wall-clock jump can let two processes hold the lock.
why: These are the 'edge cases that remain' the teacher mentioned, stated by the vendor.

text: Kleppmann's rule of thumb: if a lock exists only for efficiency (avoiding duplicate work), a single Redis instance is enough. If it protects correctness, use a consensus system such as ZooKeeper with fencing tokens rather than Redlock.
why: Helps readers choose between single-instance Redis, Redlock and a consensus-based lock.

text: Long jobs don't need a long TTL. The holder can extend the lease while it is still working (Redis: a Lua script that resets the TTL only if the key still holds its value). The DynamoDB Lock Client does the same with periodic heartbeats against a lease (example: 3 s heartbeat, 10 s lease).
why: Directly answers the student's concern that a TTL caps how long a process can run.

text: MySQL has named locks built in: GET_LOCK('q7', timeout) returns 1 if acquired. The lock is released by RELEASE_LOCK() or 'implicitly when your session terminates (either normally or abnormally)', so a crashed holder does not leave a perpetual lock. It is local to a single mysqld.
why: A ready-made MySQL lock that removes the need for a TTL cron job in many cases.

text: ZooKeeper's lock recipe: each client creates an ephemeral sequential znode under the lock path. The lowest sequence number holds the lock, and every other client watches only the node just before it, so a release wakes exactly one waiter, with no polling or timeouts. Ephemeral nodes are deleted when the holder's session ends.
why: Shows concretely how the ZooKeeper lock differs from the polling Redis loop.

text: SQS standard queues are at-least-once: a copy of a message can come back if a server was unavailable during delete. A message also becomes visible again if processing outlasts the visibility timeout. AWS asks consumers to be idempotent; RabbitMQ likewise says consumers 'must be prepared to handle redeliveries'.
why: Corrects the impression that real queues make duplicate processing impossible.

text: In a MongoDB transaction, a conflicting lock request does not wait for commit: by default it waits up to 5 ms, then the transaction aborts and the client retries. A non-transactional write to a document locked by a transaction does wait until the transaction ends.
why: Gives the actual MongoDB behaviour behind the lecture's lock-manager example.

text: TCP alone may not detect a dead peer quickly. If the client's host crashes or is cut off, the server's socket stays open until the application times out or TCP keepalive fires. On Linux, keepalive is off unless SO_KEEPALIVE is set and starts only after 7200 s idle by default.
why: Shows why even a connection-based lock still needs a lease/timeout.

text: dpkg's lock is not 'does the file exist?'. Frontends take an fcntl(2) advisory record lock on <admindir>/lock-frontend and then <admindir>/lock (/var/lib/dpkg on Debian/Ubuntu). The kernel drops such locks automatically when the process terminates, so a crash never leaves a stale lock.
why: Shows how the OS solves the 'holder died' problem for processes, the same problem TTL solves for remote locks.

text: For scale: a round trip inside one datacenter is about 0.5 ms (Jeff Dean's ~2012 figures), and AWS describes latency between Availability Zones in a region as single-digit milliseconds. Most of the 3-10 ms per service hop is therefore serialization, TLS, queueing and handler time, not the wire.
why: Gives readers realistic latency numbers to budget hops.
